narrative:
The model predicted a 72.9% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability is well above the acceptance threshold, your law school application was rejected.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors, ranked by importance. Your first-year and third-year class rankings had the strongest influence, both pushing the prediction strongly toward failure. Being in the bottom decile for grades in both Year 1 and Year 3 placed you far below the average student who was accepted (who typically ranked around the 6th decile). These consistently low academic standings in law school were the main reasons the model doubted your likelihood of passing the bar.

Your LSAT score of 35 was the third most important factor. While this score is only slightly below the 37.2 average of accepted students and therefore worked mildly in your favor, it was not nearly enough to offset the much larger negative impact of your class rankings.

Your undergraduate GPA, family income in the upper-middle bracket, and plan to attend full-time were considered but had far less influence on the outcome.

To improve your chances, you should focus on raising your academic performance if you retake any courses, or consider retaking the LSAT to achieve a significantly higher score. Strengthening these key areas will be the most effective way to demonstrate readiness for the bar exam in any future applications. (218 words)
